Every request to a language model is billed in tokens, not words or characters. A token is a fragment the model's tokenizer carved out of your text: sometimes a whole word, sometimes a syllable, sometimes a single punctuation mark. Common English words usually map to one token each, while rare words, names and numbers split into several. That is why two prompts of the same length on screen can cost noticeably different amounts, and why the same prompt costs different amounts on different providers. Each provider trains its own tokenizer, so the same sentence becomes a different number of pieces depending on who is reading it.

Output tokens matter even more than input. Most providers charge several times more per output token than per input token, so a model that answers in three paragraphs instead of one can triple the cost of an otherwise identical request. A system prompt that is sent with every single request is the other quiet expense: it is small per call and enormous at scale, which is exactly what prompt caching was invented to fix.
